query: A Lid on the Pot In the market you find her at the charm seller's stall. He's holding up a grey glass bead on a cord. "Lumenhold-blessed," he's saying. "Smothers it, like a lid on a pot. No more flares, no more fuss." It's plain glass; you can see that from here. She's counting out her savings. Let her believe in it You say nothing. She buys it and puts it on. It's only glass, but she believes in it, and the sugar pans stay cold all week. She looks lighter, and smaller. Tell her it's only glass "It's glass," you tell her. "You did the hard part yourself, out past the fields." The charm seller gives you the look of a man revising his prices. She puts her coins back in her apron, slowly. She buys it anyway. "Easy for you," she says, not unkindly. "You get to go back."
